## Applied Exercises

Work on these exercises in CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite, and save the queries of each exercise in a script of its own, named after the exercise (such as `Ex 12.1.sql`). Give each script the structure of the audit query library: a header comment, then one section per test that states its objective, population, reconciliation, and expected result. Record a disposition for every exception you find.

### Financial Accounting Exercises

**Exercise 12.1: Cutoff at Each Year-End**

**Table group:** Order-to-Cash, Procure-to-Pay, Accounting Core

**Scenario.** Tutorial 12.1 found sales invoices posted in a later fiscal year than their date. The controller asks for the effect on each year's revenue, and for the same test on the supplier side, before the fiscal 2026 statements are finalized.

**Requirements.**

(1) List the sales invoices whose revenue postings fall in a different fiscal year from the invoice date, with their SubTotal, GrandTotal, and the two dates.

(2) For each fiscal year, total the revenue recorded in that year for invoices dated in the year before, and the revenue dated in that year but recorded in the next one. Calculate the net effect of cutoff on each year's revenue.

(3) Repeat the test for supplier invoices, comparing InvoiceDate with the posting date of each invoice's ledger rows. Compare the posting dates with ReceivedDate, and explain which date Charles River posts supplier invoices on.

(4) Write a short memo (one half page) to the controller with the effect on each year and a recommendation for the year-end close.

**Deliverable.** A script with the cutoff tests and a half-page memo.

**Exercise 12.2: The Accrual for Goods Received Not Invoiced**

**Table group:** Procure-to-Pay, Accounting Core

**Scenario.** Tutorial 12.2 reconciled the receipts not yet invoiced to account 2020 in total. The controller asks for the detail behind the balance at the end of fiscal 2026: which suppliers it is owed to, how old the receipts are, and which purchases are billed without a purchase order at all.

**Requirements.**

(1) List the goods receipt lines not fully invoiced at the end of fiscal 2026, valued at their receipt value for the part not yet invoiced, with the supplier and the receipt date.

(2) Total the value by supplier and list the five largest, and total it by receipt month.

(3) Identify the receipts more than two months old at the year-end, and suggest why each might not yet be invoiced.

(4) Find the supplier invoice lines that have no purchase order line. Total them by item group, and check whether each is linked to an accrual journal entry. Explain how these purchases should be tested, since a three-way match cannot apply to them.

(5) Write a short memo (one half page) to the controller on the accrual and the purchases without orders.

**Deliverable.** A script with the accrual detail and a half-page memo.

### Managerial Accounting Exercises

**Exercise 12.3: Where Did the Time Go?**

**Table group:** Manufacturing

**Scenario.** Tutorial 11.2 showed Packing and Quality Assurance recording several times their planned hours, and Tutorial 12.3 showed that much of the time was recorded after operations had ended. The plant manager asks what the work-center comparison looks like when only the time recorded while each operation was open is counted.

**Requirements.**

(1) For each direct labor time entry, flag whether it was recorded on or before the operation's ActualEndDate.

(2) Repeat the work-center comparison of Tutorial 11.2, with the planned hours of each work center and year, and two recorded-to-planned ratios: one for all direct hours, and one for the hours recorded while the operation was open.

(3) Rank the work centers by each ratio, and describe how the ranking changes.

(4) Total the direct hours of each year by work date, and compare them with the indirect time of Tutorial 10.3. Explain where the extra paid hours of Chapter 10 were recorded.

(5) Write a short memo (one half page) to the plant manager: what the operation-level data can and cannot support, and what should change in how time is recorded.

**Deliverable.** A script with the comparison and a half-page memo.

<!-- Instructor notes, Exercise 12.3: counting only the time recorded while the operation was open, every work center falls below plan in

     0.39, 0.40, 0.55, 4.07, 3.92). In 2024 the in-window ratios were 0.62, 0.55, 0.68, 0.38, 1.28. The Packing excess disappears, which
     shows that it came from time charged after the operation ended; Packing is the last operation of every routing, so late time lands

     23,200 to 35,800 and 38,500, so the extra paid hours of Chapter 10 were recorded as indirect time; the late direct time is misplaced

     the plant-level measure of Chapter 11 is unaffected. -->


**Exercise 12.4: Is the Overtime Approval Doing Its Job?**

**Table group:** Manufacturing, Payroll

**Scenario.** Tutorial 12.3 found that overtime above half an hour is almost always approved. The controller wants to know whether the approvals are a real control over the growth in overtime, or only a record that it happened.

**Requirements.**

(1) Count the overtime approvals by year and reason code, and describe how the mix of reasons changed as overtime grew.

(2) Count the approvals by approver and job title, and calculate the share approved by the largest approver.

(3) Compare each approval's ApprovedHours with its RequestedHours, and its ApprovedDate with the WorkDate of the overtime.

(4) Explain what the results say about the design of the overtime approval control, and suggest two changes that would make it a real control.

**Deliverable.** A script with the analysis and a short list of findings and recommendations.

<!-- Instructor notes, Exercise 12.4: 18,145 approvals, spread almost evenly over four reason codes in every year (Backlog Recovery, Late
     Operation, Load Surge, Month-End Support; about a quarter each), so the reasons carry no information about why overtime grew. The
     Production Manager approved 16,676 approvals (about 92%). Every approval grants exactly the hours requested, and every approval is
     dated on the work date itself, so no request was ever reduced or approved in advance. The control records overtime rather than
     authorizing it: approval in advance, a limit per employee and week, and informative reasons reviewed by someone outside production
     would make it a control. -->


### Auditing Exercises

**Exercise 12.5: Duplicate Payments in SQL**

**Table group:** Procure-to-Pay

**Scenario.** Chapter 2 promised that the duplicate payment analysis of Exercise 2.6 would be completed in SQL. The chief audit executive asks you to run the full set of duplicate tests on the supplier payments and invoices of fiscal 2024 through 2026, and to add them to the query library.

**Requirements.**

(1) Find the supplier invoice numbers that appear more than once for the same supplier, and list both invoices of each pair with their amounts and payments.

(2) Exercise 2.6 warned that the same invoice could be entered with a slightly different number. Repeat test (1) on standardized invoice numbers, using UPPER, TRIM, and REPLACE to remove differences of case, spaces, and hyphens, and report whether it finds any pair that the exact test missed.

(3) Find the check numbers used more than once for the same supplier.

(4) Use a self-join to find pairs of payments to the same supplier for the same amount on different dates within 30 days of each other, dated through 2026-12-31. Report whether any pair pays the same invoice.

(5) For each test, record the number of exceptions and a disposition, and explain why a self-join is needed for the fourth test but not for the others.

**Deliverable.** A script with the four tests and a table of results and dispositions.

     find the same six pairs and no others: the numbers are entered consistently. (3) Two check numbers are used twice, both for

**Exercise 12.6: Sequence and First-Digit Tests in SQL**

**Table group:** Order-to-Cash, Procure-to-Pay, Accounting Core

**Scenario.** The chief audit executive wants the sequence and first-digit tests of Chapter 8 in the query library, so that they run on every document series each quarter without a workbook.

**Requirements.**

(1) For the sales invoice, purchase order, cash receipt, and journal entry numbers, extract the year and the sequence number with SUBSTR and CAST. Use LAG, partitioned by year, to find any step greater than one, and report the first and last number of each year.

(2) Describe which series restart their numbering each year and which continue across years.

(3) Calculate the first significant digit of every supplier payment dated through 2026-12-31 with `printf('%e', Amount)`, and the actual and expected proportion of each digit, using `LOG10(1 + 1.0 / Digit)`.

(4) Calculate the mean absolute deviation for all payments, for full payments (Amount equal to the invoice's GrandTotal), and for partial payments, and compare the results with Tutorial 8.1.

(5) Write a short note on the advantage of running these tests in SQL rather than in a workbook.

**Deliverable.** A script with the sequence and first-digit tests and a short note.
